name: Model Context Protocol
summary: An open protocol specification and TypeScript-first schema for connecting host applications to servers through JSON-RPC sessions, capability negotiation, and composable resources, prompts, and tools. This card targets the protocol/specification repository, not an MCP language SDK.
scope: resources, prompts, tools, and transport boundary

features.name: Host, client, and server role separation
features.description: The official architecture documentation separates a host application from one or more clients and specialized servers. Clients attach to servers, while servers expose focused context and capabilities; the host retains orchestration and security responsibility.
benefits: Allows one host to compose multiple specialized servers
Keeps server capabilities bounded by explicit protocol connections
costs: Cross-server orchestration and consent remain host responsibilities
Role separation does not itself guarantee authorization or safe tool behavior

features.name: JSON-RPC session and capability negotiation
features.description: The fixed schema defines JSON-RPC request/response/notification types, initialization fields, client and server capabilities, and feature declarations for prompts, resources, and tools. The official specification describes stateful connections and negotiated capabilities.
benefits: Provides a typed wire contract with explicit initialization and feature discovery
Allows clients and servers to evolve through declared capabilities
costs: Version and capability mismatches require explicit failure handling
A negotiated capability is an interface declaration, not proof that the implementation is secure or available

features.name: Composable resources, prompts, and tools
features.description: The protocol specification defines server-side resources, prompts, and tools as distinct primitives, while the schema gives each a typed protocol representation. Their separation lets a host present context, templates, and executable actions through one protocol family.
benefits: Supports composition of read context, user-facing templates, and model-invoked actions
Keeps primitive-specific discovery and invocation semantics explicit
costs: Tools can reach arbitrary code or data and need user consent and authorization
Different primitives have different lifecycle, streaming, and error semantics

features.name: Transport and security boundary
features.description: The official specification uses JSON-RPC over protocol transports and places consent, authorization, privacy, and tool-safety responsibilities primarily on hosts and implementors. The card records these as protocol boundary guidance, not as automatic enforcement by the wire format.
benefits: Makes transport and trust assumptions visible to implementors
Preserves host control over data sharing and tool invocation
costs: Protocol messages cannot enforce all policy or prevent malicious server behavior
Remote transports and server-initiated capabilities expand the trust boundary

mathematical_views.question: How do initialization, capability declaration, requests, notifications, and shutdown define a valid MCP session?
assumptions: A session carries protocol version and capability information
Requests and notifications follow JSON-RPC message rules
Only declared capabilities are assumed available
The model abstracts transport framing and authentication

mathematical_views.question: How can one host compose resources, prompts, and tools from multiple servers without treating them as the same operation?
assumptions: Clients connect host applications to specialized servers
Resources, prompts, and tools remain distinct primitive types
The host controls context presentation and authorization decisions
The view does not claim cross-server atomicity

mathematical_views.question: Where do consent and authorization obligations enter when a model uses a server-exposed tool?
assumptions: Tool descriptions and annotations are untrusted unless obtained from a trusted server
Hosts obtain user consent before tool invocation according to official security guidance
The protocol schema cannot prove the safety of arbitrary tool implementations

benefits: Composable specialized servers under host control
costs: Orchestration and trust remain distributed across the host and servers

benefits: Distinct primitives for context, templates, and actions
costs: Multiple primitive lifecycles and security semantics must be reconciled
Wire protocol cannot replace host authorization and operational hardening
